caption: Fig. 1: DETR directly predicts (in parallel) the final set of detections by combining a common CNN with a transformer architecture. During training, bipartite matching uniquely assigns predictions with ground truth boxes. Prediction with no match should yield a ' no object ' ( ∅ ) class prediction.
description: This figure is a diagram showing the architecture of the DETR model for object detection. It consists of a CNN, a transformer encoder-decoder, and a bipartite matching loss. The input image is processed by the CNN to extract features, which are then fed into the transformer encoder-decoder to generate box predictions. The bipartite matching loss is used during training to assign predictions to ground truth boxes. The figure shows the flow of data from the input image to the final set of detections.

caption: Fig. 2: DETR uses a conventional CNN backbone to learn a 2D representation of an input image. The model flattens it and supplements it with a positional encoding before passing it into a transformer encoder. A transformer decoder then takes as input a small fixed number of learned positional embeddings, which we call object queries , and additionally attends to the encoder output. We pass each output embedding of the decoder to a shared feed forward network (FFN) that predicts either a detection (class and bounding box) or a ' no object ' class.
description:
Figure type: Diagram
Description: The diagram illustrates the architecture of the DETR model for object detection. It shows a conventional CNN backbone that processes the input image to create a 2D representation. This representation is flattened and combined with positional encoding before being passed into a transformer encoder. The transformer decoder takes a fixed number of learned positional embeddings (object queries) and attends to the encoder output. Each output embedding from the decoder is processed by a shared feed-forward network (FFN) to predict either a detection (class and bounding box) or a 'no object' class.

caption: Fig. 4: AP and AP 50 performance after each decoder layer. A single long schedule baseline model is evaluated. DETR does not need NMS by design, which is validated by this figure. NMS lowers AP in the final layers, removing TP predictions, but improves AP in the first decoder layers, removing double predictions, as there is no communication in the first layer, and slightly improves AP 50 .

caption: Fig. 7: Visualization of all box predictions on all images from COCO 2017 val set for 20 out of total N = 100 prediction slots in DETR decoder. Each box prediction is represented as a point with the coordinates of its center in the 1-by-1 square normalized by each image size. The points are color-coded so that green color corresponds to small boxes, red to large horizontal boxes and blue to large vertical boxes. We observe that each slot learns to specialize on certain areas and box sizes with several operating modes. We note that almost all slots have a mode of predicting large image-wide boxes that are common in COCO dataset.
